newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S. envoy in Zaire, urges negotiation to end war.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy in Zaire, urges negotiation to end war.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson arrived in Zaire on Monday and declared the United States wanted to see a negotiated settlement in the Central African nation's seven-month-old civil war.

"The United States firmly believes that there can be no military solution to the crisis, but rather a negotiated settlement leading to an inclusive transitional government and fair and free elections," Richardson said in a statement.

"I am also here because of our grave concern for the plight of several thousand refugees and displaced Zaireans. There is a humanitarian crisis here and the international community must respond," added Richardson.
He said he would meet embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko on Tuesday morning and then travel to Lubumbashi, in rebel-held territory, on Wednesday to see guerrilla leader Laurent Kabila.
Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, also signalled a toughening of U.S. attitude towards Kabila over the the controversial issue of Hutu refugees central to the war.

"There have been some reports of massacres and human rights abuses. This must end," he said, adding: "Internatonal aid organisations and the United Nations must have immediate access to people in need. During my visit I will press for this."

Richardson arrived in Zaire a day after Kabila agreed during emergency talks to give aid agencies access to nearly 100,000 Hutu refugees who fled camps in rebel-held territory when they came under armed attack last week.
His arrival also concided with reports that rebels advancing on Kinshasa were closing in on the provincial town of Kikwit 400 km (250 miles) from the capital.

Earlier, Mobutu's son and adviser, Nzanga Mobutu, told Reuters that Richardson was bringing a personal message from President Bill Clinton to Mobutu, which he would deliver to the Zairean leader at his camp Tshatshi residence.
"He is carrying a personal letter from President Clinton. We don't know yet what it contains," Nzanga said.
Richardson declined to answer reporters' questions on efforts to bring Mobutu and Kabila together for talks aimed at preventing war reaching the Zaire capital.
Mobutu and Kabila have agreed to meet but determining a neutral venue is a problem as is Kabila's insistence that the only item on the agenda be Mobutu's departure.

Kabila insists Mobutu come either to Zambia or South Africa. Mobutu, who is convalescing after prostate cancer surgery in August, wants a venue closer to home. He previously suggested the Congo capital Brazzaville across the river from Kinshasa.
Zaire has accused Zambia of aiding the rebels and looked unlikely to consider the country as a neutral venue.
Both the White House and the State Department have been calling for Mobutu, who has ruled the vast Central African country for 32 years, to give way to a transitional government.

Mobutu's MPR party accuses Washington of sponsoring Tutsi-led rebels who control more than half the country and party leaders drummed up an anti-U.S. campaign at a rally and on state media on the eve of Richardson's arrival.

International efforts to stage direct talks between the two foes have intensified as rebels step up their advance on Kinshasa. Rebel leaders say they expect the capital to fall within days. Government army commanders say they will fight to the death to defend the city.
